_about: Storybook retellings of the field guide, one per named card, written at a preteen/teen reading level (Steve, 2026-09-08: 'each element its own title, a few paragraphs and a generated image'). The GUIDE is canon; these are retellings of it and must never contradict it. When a new guide draft lands, re-read each story against its card and refresh this file (guide_sha1 says which draft they were written from). image_prompt = the scene for the page's illustration (story_plates.py adds the shared style). preface = the map page's introduction. Placeholder slots get no story. motifs = the node's arcane motifs (canon/STYLE.md: symbols painted on walls, wires out of trees, the card's disturbance) for the hybrid plate prompt. source_photo = the master drawing's locked source photograph (EV id), set only where the node has no tagged photo yet (T75 interim) or to override the auto pick. hook = the one line under the video slot (site review FB-01/24). no_rule = explicit per-node exception (print no rule). draft_note = a retelling ahead of the guide, flagged in reports. video_url = the chapter's YouTube URL when the video is published (the video slot; the master plate holds it until then). redirects = old slug → new slug (build_site.py writes a tiny redirect page at the old dir). credits = the discreet creator / tool line in every colophon (Steve, 2026-09-11). MIRROR: paragraphs + hook + title come from canon/story/story.json (mirror_story.py) — never edit them here; chapter_sha1 = the chapter they mirror.
north_star: THE CITY MUST NOT FALL SILENT.
preface: Terminal City is a parallel city. It shares every street, wire, rooftop and shoreline with Vancouver, and most people only ever see Vancouver. Underneath, Terminal City keeps the music, the art and the strange ideas moving so that the city never falls silent. The two worlds are not meant to cross, except in one direction: through the outputs. A soundtrack that adjusts itself on the wires. A piece of street art a citizen happens to see. A late-night door that turns out to be the right one. Those are the only places Terminal City is allowed to touch ordinary life, and nobody who is touched by it is supposed to know. Nobody rules it. It is not finished, and it never will be. Every day it is inspected, repaired, handed over and rebuilt, and every morning it starts again at Trout Lake. These are its nineteen parts.

morning-meeting.title: The Morning Meeting
paragraphs: Every morning, before the sun comes up, a thin mist lies on Trout Lake. It hangs in the reeds and drifts over the glassy water, so light you could walk through it and not notice. This is where the day's first meeting happens, and almost nobody sees it. If you walked past, you would see a murder of crows in a tree by the water and one weathered street artist on a bench, paint on their hands and their jacket, feeding them. That is the whole meeting. That is exactly what it is supposed to look like.

The crows are reporting. They spent yesterday over the whole city, roofs, wires, walls, parks, the edges where the streets meet the water, and they have noticed which corners have gone quiet and where music and art and attention are running thin. They do not speak English. The artist on the bench understands anyway.

There is no chairperson, no agenda and no minutes. The meeting decides what the city needs today. Then the crows lift off, the artist picks up their bucket, and the water goes still. Somewhere behind them, without anyone noticing, the mist begins to move.
morning-meeting.image_prompt: Trout Lake in East Vancouver just before sunrise, glassy still water, a murder of crows gathered on the grass and in a bare tree by the shore with unusual collective focus, all facing one tired, ordinary-looking person in paint-spattered work clothes sitting on a park bench and feeding them, a paint bucket beside the bench, the whole scene easy to mistake for someone feeding birds, distant city lights across the water.
morning-meeting.motifs: Wires grow out of the bare tree the crows sit in and run down into the reeds; a faint circle of engraved geometry lies on the still water with no source.
morning-meeting.hook: Before sunrise, someone feeds the crows at Trout Lake. That is the whole meeting.

morning-mist.title: Morning Mist
paragraphs: Some mornings the whole city wakes up knowing the same thing, and nobody said it. Before sunrise a thin mist drifts out of Trout Lake, where it waited through the meeting, and settles over every district. It catches on telephone wires, wet paint, rails, glass, seawall lamps and the branches of trees.

It carries no instructions. Nothing is written in the air. But watch what happens under it. A painter turns toward a wall she was not going to paint today. A radio three streets away changes its tone at the same moment. A lamp on the seawall seems to lean into its post. Things that have nothing to do with each other change together, quietly, as if they had all been told.
That is how you spot it. Not by the weather, which is only Vancouver weather, but by the way the city agrees with itself all at once. The mist carries what is needed, not how to do it.
morning-mist.image_prompt: East Vancouver back lanes at first light with thin mist drifting over rooftops, utility poles and wires, wet footprints on the pavement leading toward an open window, and one dry patch of asphalt shaped like a small lake.
morning-mist.motifs: The mist is drawn as fine engraved lines threading through the wires and along the lanes; one painted glyph on a garage wall is catching the mist first.
morning-mist.hook: Some mornings the whole city wakes up knowing the same thing, and nobody said it.

wire-choir.title: The Wire Choir
paragraphs: Look up in an East Van lane: telephone poles, layers of wires, trolley lines, transformers. Add every radio, every car stereo, every pair of headphones and the bass leaking under a warehouse door, and you have the Wire Choir. It is how Terminal City sings to itself.

When a neighbourhood goes quiet, the Choir leans on coincidence. Somebody's car at a red light is playing the exact song. A band is rehearsing through a wall you happen to be leaning on. A radio in an upstairs apartment, a window left open, a snatch of something from a loading bay at two in the morning. You still choose what you listen to. You really did. The timing was just a little too good.

It cannot reach everywhere. Inside Stanley Park the signal fades into the trees. And whatever people make out of what they heard, a track, a night out, a wall of paint, comes back into the wires and keeps the city from falling silent. No one hears the broadcast as an announcement.
wire-choir.image_prompt: A dense tangle of overhead trolley wires, power lines and transformers above an East Vancouver street, the wires briefly lining up into the shape of a sound wave, a speaker cone strapped to a utility pole, faint lines of sound spreading along the wires.
wire-choir.motifs: Wires come out of the trees along the street and join the pole lines; the overhead wires resolve into a waveform and a glyph; a pair of headphones hangs from a wire.
wire-choir.hook: The right song, at the right moment, out of somebody else's window.

clock.title: The Clock
paragraphs: Terminal City calls the SkyTrain the Clock. All day it moves above and beneath the streets, closing doors, sounding chimes, crossing itself and pulling away again. Thousands of people use it to get somewhere. Almost none of them notice what else it is doing.
The trains do not follow the rhythm of the city. The city follows the trains.

A door closes at Commercial–Broadway and, somewhere across town, a light changes. A train enters a station just as music starts behind an apartment window. Two trains pass each other above the street and a hundred unrelated things seem to happen together.

Usually the coincidences are small enough to ignore. A pedestrian reaches the curb exactly as the signal changes. Rain begins between two songs. The beat in your headphones lands perfectly beneath the door chime. Once you notice it, you start noticing it everywhere.
The Clock does not tell Terminal City what time it is. It distributes time. As long as the trains keep their rhythm, distant parts of the city remain close enough to agree on when now is.

Occasionally the Clock drifts. Only by a second or two. That's enough. Music feels slightly late. People arrive just after someone has left. Conversations overlap. Crosswalks seem impatient. Repair People stop what they're doing and look toward the tracks.
Then a train passes. The doors close. The city catches up.
clock.image_prompt: A SkyTrain running along its elevated concrete guideway above a corridor of trees and low rooftops, seen from the street below, a station platform with a hanging sign that shows only a blank shape, a large platform clock, a few small figures looking up and setting their watches.
clock.motifs: Engraved timing geometry radiates from the guideway; a platform clock with hands but no numbers; a small painted symbol on the pillar beneath the line.
clock.hook: Every city needs a clock. Vancouver rides inside its.
clock.author_note: story = Steve's own text verbatim (sas-project-mgmt/canon/drafts/the-clock-2026-09-10.md), his one-line paragraphs grouped; the first two sentences are the hook

probes.title: The Probes
paragraphs: Down at the port, the giant cranes stand along the water. To most people they are machinery. In Terminal City they are the Probes, and they are not loading ships. They are listening to somewhere else.

Ships leave the harbour with questions. They come back with weather, objects, languages, sounds, rumours, materials and patterns nobody here has seen before, and the cranes lift it all ashore. Sometimes the cargo is only the box the information travelled in.
Without the Probes the city would only ever feed on itself. If you see a crane turned to face inland instead of the sea, it has learned something. What did you see?
probes.image_prompt: Giant harbour gantry cranes along the port of Vancouver with hooks shaped like antennas, one crane turned to face inland, a container ship beneath them, faint radio waves rising from the hooks, mountains and fog beyond the inlet.
probes.motifs: The crane hooks are antennas; engraved signal arcs rise from one crane turned inland; a painted glyph on a container.
probes.hook: The cranes are not loading ships. They are listening to somewhere else.

old-line.title: The Old Line
paragraphs: Vancouver has taken a lot of routes off its maps: streetcar rails, rail spurs, stops that used to matter. On wet nights they come back. Look into a puddle on a street with no tracks and you may see rails shining in the reflection.

This is the Old Line. It does not run on a timetable and it does not care what the current map says. Old alignments, old rights-of-way, old versions of a corner, all still there under the asphalt, all still in use. A car on the Old Line stops where a place used to matter, not where a passenger expects.

The Freight shares its rails but does the opposite job: the Freight removes what cannot stay, and the Old Line keeps what must not be forgotten. You may follow an old route. You may not assume it goes where the current map says.
old-line.image_prompt: Commercial Drive at night after rain, old streetcar rails shining in the puddles where no track exists on the street, an old interurban tram car with no route number arriving out of the dark under a web of trolley wires, shop awnings and reflections.
old-line.motifs: Rails shine in the wet reflections where the street has none; small painted repair sigils mark old stops on the walls; wires drop from a street tree.
old-line.hook: On wet nights the puddles show rails the street no longer has.

repair-people.title: The Repair People
paragraphs: Painters, graffiti writers, sticker makers, paste-up crews, photographers, muralists, anyone up a ladder at an odd hour with a bucket and work clothes. Some of them are Repair People. Most are not. You cannot tell which.

A Repair Person treats a crack in a wall the way a plumber treats a burst pipe. What the city sees as a tag, a sticker, a mural or a fresh coat of paint may be structural maintenance. They are hard to get to know. Ask one a question and you will get a short answer and a person already turning back to the work. Nobody knows exactly what they are, and the city has decided not to ask.

They take their priorities from the Morning Meeting and their odd ideas from the Green Static. Everything they fix stays visible, because that is the point: the repair is also the art, and the art is what keeps people noticing.
repair-people.image_prompt: An East Vancouver alley wall layered with murals, posters and stickers, a figure seen from behind on a ladder painting one bold brushstroke across a real crack in the brickwork so that the stroke holds the wall together, paint cans, a roller and a bucket below.
repair-people.motifs: The wall is covered in painted symbols that read as occult geometry, one bold mark continuing across a real crack and off the wall into space.
repair-people.hook: Some of the people painting the walls are holding the city together. You cannot tell which.

crows.title: Crows
paragraphs: Every evening the crows cross Vancouver in one long, loose stream, heading east to roost, and every morning they come back. It looks like a commute because it is one. The crows are Terminal City's inspectors, and they are going home after a long shift.

During the day they check everything: roofs, wires, streets, parks, rails, walls, the edges of the city. They notice the corner that has gone quiet, the wall that has cracked, the boundary that has gone soft. They do not write it down. They carry it to Trout Lake before dawn.

They are reliable, collective, and blue-collar to the bone, but they are still crows: no uniforms, no lunch pails, no English. If you see a whole flock facing the same point at once, they have found something.
crows.image_prompt: A long loose formation of crows crossing the dawn sky over East Vancouver rooftops and utility poles, one crow standing perfectly still on a wire in the foreground, an old punch-card time clock mounted on the pole beneath it.
crows.motifs: Every crow faces the same point; the wires the flock crosses are also growing out of a tree; a punch-clock glyph is painted on the pole.
crows.hook: Every evening the crows go home from work.

sunset.title: Sunset
paragraphs: In Terminal City the sunset is a shift change. All day the city has been inspected and patched and kept in time. As the light goes through the wires and over the rooftops, the Repair People put their brushes down, the crows head home, and the daytime systems hand the city over to the night.

You feel it without knowing why. Around sunset people want to stop working, walk, meet someone, eat, listen to something, make something, go out. That is not an accident. Maintenance is not the point of the city. Maintenance exists so that people can eventually stop working, and the sunset is the moment they are allowed to.
The Nocturnals start scouting. The Wire Choir shifts from daytime traffic to night music. The other city clocks in.
sunset.image_prompt: A western horizon of water seen past East Vancouver rooftops, utility poles and wires, the sun sinking as a half circle with one line beneath it, a second fainter horizon line drawn above the real one, streetlights already lit, a few people watching from a rooftop and from the seawall.
sunset.motifs: A second, fainter engraved horizon line above the real one; streetlights already lit; a symbol painted on the rooftop parapet the watchers stand behind.
sunset.hook: Maintenance is not the point of the city.

sixth-hour.title: The Sixth Hour
paragraphs: The Sixth Hour is not six o'clock. It is the sixth hour of music without a break. Some warehouse rooms in East Van are perfectly ordinary for the first five hours. After that, they get less reliable.

By the sixth hour, distance stretches. The walls breathe by a few millimetres. A door is not quite where it was. Nothing dramatic happens, and nobody could photograph it, but everyone in the room feels the rules of space go soft. Terminal City lets this happen on purpose. Nobody has decided whether it is a malfunction or a pressure release, and nobody in the room is asking.
The Nocturnals find the room. The Wire Choir carries the signal without admitting it. Whatever gets bent tonight goes on the crows' list tomorrow. The sixth hour starts when the music does.
sixth-hour.image_prompt: An anonymous windowless East Vancouver warehouse at night on wet pavement, a single small door glowing bright with light spilling out onto the ground, bass waves rippling the brickwork around it, a small painted mark beside the door, a coyote waiting patiently outside.
sixth-hour.motifs: Engraved bass rings ripple the brickwork around the door; a painted sigil marks the door; wires reach the warehouse from a tree across the lot.
sixth-hour.hook: The sixth hour of music, when the walls start to breathe.

nocturnals.title: The Nocturnals
paragraphs: Something already knows where tonight is. After sunset, before anyone has heard of the room, a set of tracks crosses a wet service road toward it. A shadow moves along a rail cut. A coyote is already waiting at a warehouse door nobody has told you about. In Terminal City these are the Nocturnals: the night scouts.

They are not a council and not a workforce. They are whatever reliably leads you to the right unmarked door, and they are gone before you can thank them. People follow without meaning to, one coincidence at a time, and end up somewhere the wider city has not noticed yet.
They take the handoff from the Sunset and lead toward the Sixth Hour. The Green Static, which confuses every scheduled system in the city, does not confuse them at all.
nocturnals.image_prompt: An East Vancouver service road and rail cut at night, wet pavement, chain-link fence and a loading bay, a trail of animal tracks in the wet leading toward one unmarked warehouse door with a thin line of light under it, only the shadow of an animal slipping out of the edge of the picture, the feeling of being led somewhere, no people.
nocturnals.motifs: Paw prints and engraved guide-lines lead to the one door; a painted symbol beside it; wires from a tree over the fence run to the loading bay.

nocturnals.hook: Something already knows where tonight is.

terminal-fog.title: Terminal Fog
paragraphs: The Repair People patch the city all day, one wall at a time. Some things cannot be patched. For those, Terminal City has the fog.

Late at night, after the after-hours rooms have emptied and the Freight has taken away what cannot stay, fog comes in from the water. It covers the shoreline, the tracks, the lights, the skyline, until enough of Vancouver is hidden for Terminal City to be rebuilt underneath. This is the full rebuild, the one that fixes what a brush cannot.

When the fog lifts, the city is back. Almost. One familiar thing is gone, or shifted, or slightly wrong, and nobody announces it. Then the crows fly out to inspect the new build, and the cycle returns to Trout Lake.
terminal-fog.image_prompt: A great bank of fog rolling in from the harbour and swallowing ship masts, a crane tip, downtown towers and rail lines, everything dissolving into blank white paper, while in the foreground a small still lake with reeds and one crow remains the last visible place.
terminal-fog.motifs: The fog is drawn as engraved smoke lines erasing one building completely; a glyph on the last visible wall at the lake.
terminal-fog.hook: The fog takes the city apart and puts it back almost right.

eternal-night.title: Eternal Night
paragraphs: Not every part of the city gets looked at. Sealed doors, empty windows, a sign for a shop that closed years ago, a painting on a wall nobody walks past anymore. Where attention has withdrawn, the night stays, even at noon. This is the Eternal Night.

It is not a place so much as a condition, and it is the one thing Terminal City works against. Not a villain. Just forgetting. When people stop noticing a room, a wall, a habit a neighbourhood had, the night settles into it, and what was there goes missing, quietly, without anyone deciding it should.

The crows inspect its edges and carry them to Trout Lake. By day the Repair People are sent there; what a brush cannot fix, the fog rebuilds; what cannot be rebuilt, the Freight takes away. The Eternal Night keeps nothing. It only shows the city where it is losing.
eternal-night.image_prompt: An old brick building in the deepest hour of night with a sealed loading door, empty windows, a painted shop sign faded past reading, an old mural fading on the side wall, deep architectural shadow and rain, one window impossibly black as if it absorbs the light of the street lamp, an empty street, no people anywhere.
eternal-night.motifs: One window impossibly black, drawn as absolute ink; faded painted symbols on the sealed loading door; no people.

master.picked_by: video T94 (Draft 0.8 re-take), mirrored from masters.json

eternal-night.hook: Where nobody looks anymore, the night stays.

outer-circuit.title: The Outer Circuit
paragraphs: The seawall looks like a path. It is also the edge of the city, and edges have to be checked. Every walker, runner and cyclist on the seawall, and every person who cannot sleep and goes for a walk along the water at two in the morning, is checking it without knowing.

In Terminal City their movement is what keeps the edge in place. A person tracing the city's edge, again and again, holds that edge where it is. When the movement thins out, a stretch of path or shoreline can start to drift, or a lamp repeats itself farther around the bend than it should.
The Green Static scrambles the Circuit's signals around Stanley Park, and somewhere near Wreck Beach there is a gap it has never fully closed. The rule is the shortest one in the city.
outer-circuit.image_prompt: The Vancouver seawall curving away at blue hour, a wet path with water on one side and the city on the other, a row of old lamp posts repeating into the distance and disappearing around the bend, a cyclist and a runner, one lamp post drawn a second time where it should not be.
outer-circuit.motifs: One lamp repeats farther around the bend than it should; engraved boundary geometry runs along the wall's edge; wires from a shoreline tree run into the lamps.
outer-circuit.hook: Keep moving, and the edge of the city holds.

green-static.title: Green Static
paragraphs: At the edge of Stanley Park, the Wire Choir goes quiet. Inside, it fails completely. Schedules turn approximate, clocks drift, and the ideas you were carrying in with you simply disappear. This is the Green Static, and it is the one place in Terminal City where the city cannot hear itself.

That is the point. In place of the lost signal come things nobody sent: a melody, a colour, a picture, a rhythm that refuses the grid. Artists and Repair People walk into the trees on purpose to lose the signal and see what turns up instead. Whatever they bring out is unauthorized, and unauthorized does not mean unwanted.

The Outer Circuit runs around the park but never gets in. The Nocturnals pass through it easily. Without the Green Static, the city would become perfectly synchronized, and a perfectly synchronized city is a silent one. Lose signal. Go green. Hear nothing. Bring something back.
green-static.image_prompt: A dense Stanley Park forest trail under enormous old trees and fog, radio-wave arcs arriving from the city and dissolving into leaves at the edge of the trees, a musician sitting on a fallen log with headphones on listening to nothing, a faint glow of the city far beyond the trunks.
green-static.motifs: Engraved signal arcs from the city dissolve into leaves at the tree line; wires come out of the old-growth trunks and end in nothing.
green-static.hook: The one place the city cannot hear itself.

endless-stair.title: The Endless Stair
paragraphs: At the far western edge of the city, a long wooden staircase drops through the trees toward Wreck Beach. Everyone agrees there is a beautiful beach at the bottom. Nobody agrees on how many steps it takes to get there, and the people who make it down describe the beach differently every time.

The stair is the city's way out. It feeds something Terminal City cannot make for itself: scale, sky, sea, the feeling of leaving the useful world behind for a while. People stand at the bottom and feel small and glad about it, and the city receives that too. The stairs know when you are counting. Stop, and they add steps.
The Outer Circuit cannot quite contain it. The Beyond starts somewhere past the bottom. Sometimes the fog comes up the stairs instead of in from the sea.
endless-stair.image_prompt: An impossibly long wooden staircase with railings descending through tall coastal cedar and fir trees into fog, the steps continuing far beyond what is possible, one small figure partway down counting the steps, the lowest steps fading into blank white paper.
endless-stair.motifs: The stairs continue far past what perspective allows, into blank; small counting marks carved on the rails; wires drop from the trees alongside.
endless-stair.hook: Everyone agrees there is a beach at the bottom.

beyond.title: The Beyond
paragraphs: Past the mountains, the city's signal ends, and that is where The Beyond begins: the forests, the rivers, the highways, and the temporary towns of speakers, lights and tents that appear in the wilderness for a weekend and vanish.

Vancouver people leave the grid for The Beyond and come back different. They bring rhythms the city has never played, techniques nobody here taught them, ways of being together that the streets did not have before. The Probes bring the machine version of outside news through the port. The Beyond brings the human version, on dusty cars, at dawn.
The Green Static gets people ready to receive new ideas. The Beyond supplies them. The Wire Choir sounds different for weeks after a return.
beyond.image_prompt: The North Shore mountain skyline seen past harbour cranes, wires and rooftops, with one extra ridge line drawn faintly behind the real one, a road climbing up into cloud, and in a valley beyond the mountains a small temporary camp of tents, speaker stacks and a little stage, a line of birds leaving the city and another line returning.
beyond.motifs: One extra engraved ridge behind the real mountains; a glyph of an outbound and a returning arrow in the sky; wires trail from the roadside trees toward the pass.
beyond.hook: Past the mountains the signal ends. People go anyway.

far-shore.title: Far Shore
paragraphs: Across Burrard Inlet, the lights of North Vancouver climb the lower slopes of the mountains. On the right night, seen from this side of the water, they arrange themselves into long flowing shapes, like a script in a language nobody here speaks.

Cross the bridge and they are apartments again. That is not a trick. Some things cannot be understood up close. They only resolve after a distance has been crossed: water, language, a different way of living, a few kilometres of dark. The Far Shore is where the things the city cannot understand are turned into things it can use, and the water in between is what does the work.

The Probes send their unknowns across to it. What comes back sounds different on the wires for weeks. Nobody on either side has ever read the lights aloud, and they never spell anything. They only resolve, and only from the other side.
far-shore.image_prompt: North Vancouver seen at night across Burrard Inlet from the south shore, dark mountain slopes and rows of apartment lights, a handful of the lights joined into one flowing, graceful, unreadable calligraphic curve rising like smoke, definitely not real letters or words, the pattern reflected in the water.
far-shore.motifs: A handful of the apartment lights are joined into one flowing engraved curve rising like smoke, never letters; the water carries the reflection.

far-shore.hook: Some things only make sense from across the water.

3-17-freight.title: The 3:17 Freight
paragraphs: At 3:17 in the morning, a freight train crosses the East Van rail corridor by the False Creek flats. The train does not arrive at 3:17. 3:17 arrives with the train. Every clock within earshot holds at 3:17, or turns to it, for as long as the cars are passing, and lets go when the last one has.

The Freight is how Terminal City throws things away. Failed repairs, old versions of a corner, objects that ended up in the wrong place, the residue of a long night: anything the city cannot reconcile in the current build gets loaded onto the Freight and carried out. Nobody has explained who does the loading, and the city is not in a hurry to find out. The train goes on longer than it should. Cars repeat. Which is one more reason not to count them.
The Old Line keeps what must be remembered. The Freight removes what cannot remain. When it has gone, the fog comes in behind it and the rebuild begins.
3-17-freight.image_prompt: A long freight train crossing an East Vancouver rail corridor at night beside dark industrial flats, the train stretching farther into the distance than it should with cars that seem to repeat, a rail crossing signal, and several clock faces visible in the scene (a station clock, a clock in a window, a clock on a pole) whose hands all show seventeen minutes past three, wet ground, no people.
3-17-freight.motifs: Several clock faces with hands at seventeen past three and no numbers; the cars repeat; engraved export geometry along the corridor; a painted symbol on the crossing post.
